rationale: The promise to keep the Lord's praise continually in the mouth corresponds to Hebrews' continual sacrifice of praise, explicitly described as the fruit of lips confessing His name.

Here the meek are invited to hear and rejoice while the speaker's soul is to be praised in the Lord; Psalm 68 similarly invites the poor to see and rejoice while seeking God. The groups and sensory verbs retain their different wording.

The invitation to magnify and exalt the Lord together corresponds to Paul's prayer that the community glorify God with one accord and one mouth. Both emphasize shared praise rather than an isolated speaker.

The psalmist says the Lord heard him and rescued him from all his sojourns. Jacob recalls God hearing him in affliction and preserving him on the way he traveled; the comparison concerns divine hearing and help in these distinct journey or residence settings.

The psalm connects approaching God with enlightenment and unashamed faces. Exodus describes Moses' face being glorified through speaking with God; this is a related image of divine encounter affecting the face, in a different narrative setting.
The poor man's cry, the Lord's hearing, and rescue from afflictions correspond to the distressed wanderers crying to the Lord and being rescued from their distresses in Psalm106.

The psalm promises rescue through an angel of the Lord. Peter's prison deliverance provides a particular angelic rescue: the angel leads him past guards, and Peter identifies the Lord as sending the angel to rescue him.
Peter's statement about having tasted that the Lord is good closely repeats the psalm's invitation to taste and see that the Lord is kind. The supplied translations retain good and kind respectively.

The absence of deficiency among those fearing the Lord corresponds to the blessing of the God-fearing person whose household has riches in Psalm111. Both associate reverence for the Lord with His provision.

The psalm contrasts rich people becoming poor and hungry with good things available to those seeking the Lord. Mary's song likewise joins hungry people receiving good things with rich people being sent away empty.
Those seeking the Lord will not lack good things here; Jesus tells hearers concerned about food, drink and clothing to seek God's kingdom and righteousness, with these necessities added to them.
The invitation to children to learn the fear of the Lord corresponds to Moses' teaching of commandments so that the hearers, their sons and their sons' sons may fear the Lord throughout life.
Peter's quotation begins with the person wishing to love life and see good days, matching this opening question about desiring life and seeing good days before the instructions on speech.
The latter part of Peter's quoted verse repeats the injunction to keep the tongue from evil and the lips from speaking deceit, the two speech restrictions given here.
Peter repeats the complete sequence of turning from evil, doing good, seeking peace and pursuing it. These four actions are the distinctive shared instruction.
Peter's quotation preserves the Lord's eyes upon the righteous and His ears attending their petition, matching the two images of attentive divine regard in this verse.
The closing clause in Peter's quotation repeats the Lord's face being against evildoers. The psalm's additional destruction of their remembrance is not included in Peter's quoted sentence.

The psalm testifies that the Lord rescued the righteous from all their afflictions. Paul recounts a past rescue and then expects the Lord to rescue him from every evil work and save him into His heavenly kingdom; the comparison preserves the comprehensive language and Paul's expressly heavenly horizon.

The Lord's saving nearness to the brokenhearted corresponds to Isaiah's Lord Most High giving life to the brokenhearted. The Isaiah text describes His heavenly dwelling while also giving patience and life to the distressed.

The psalm acknowledges many afflictions of the righteous while promising the Lord's rescue. Paul similarly recounts multiple persecutions and rescue from all of them, immediately adding that godly people will be persecuted.

John connects Jesus' unbroken legs with Scripture saying that a bone of His will not be broken. This corresponds to the psalm's protection of all the righteous person's bones; the comparison does not identify this as John's exclusive scriptural source.

The psalm's statement that no bone will be shattered has a concrete wording counterpart in the Passover rule forbidding the breaking of a bone. The psalm speaks of the righteous, while Exodus regulates the Passover animal.
Both passages join hope in the Lord with redemption: His servants' souls are redeemed here, while Psalm129 calls Israel to hope and promises redemption from all its lawless deeds.
David asks the Lord to fight those fighting him. Moses' assurance that the Lord will fight for Israel supplies a narrative counterpart to the request for God to undertake His people's battle.

The petition for the Lord to take weapon and shield and rise to help corresponds to Isaiah's divine intervention with arm, breastplate, helmet and vengeance. The armor pieces differ, while both portray God acting as an armed defender.
The requested reassurance, I am your salvation, corresponds to Isaiah's confession that the Lord is his Savior and became his salvation, producing trust rather than fear.
Both petitions ask that people seeking the speaker's life be ashamed and that those wishing him evil turn backward in disgrace. The combined sequence gives a close verbal parallel.

The enemies are compared to dust before the wind here; Psalm1 compares the ungodly to chaff driven away by wind. Both use windblown material for their instability, retaining the distinct dust and chaff terms.
The enemy's way is requested to become dark and slippery. Proverbs describes the ungodly walking dark ways without knowing how they stumble, combining darkness of the path with insecure footing.

The hidden trap is described as without cause and the reproach as without purpose. Lamentations likewise describes enemies hunting the sufferer like a sparrow without cause, linking unprovoked hostility with capture imagery.
The hidden snare is requested to catch its own maker. Psalm7 similarly depicts someone falling into the pit he dug, reversing the intended victim and trap-maker.
The soul's exultation in the Lord and delight in His salvation corresponds to Mary's soul magnifying the Lord and her spirit rejoicing in God her Savior.
Praise for the Lord who rescues the poor from stronger plunderers corresponds to Jeremiah's invitation to praise the Lord for rescuing a poor person's life from evildoers' hands.

The psalmist faces unjust witnesses questioning him about what he did not know. Mark describes false witnesses against Jesus whose accusations disagree, a particular narrative comparison for hostile judicial testimony.

The complaint that enemies repaid good with evil corresponds to Proverbs' warning about the person who repays evil instead of good. The proverb supplies the ethical judgment on the conduct lamented here.
Both speakers humble or bow down their souls with fasting and put on sackcloth amid reproach. The comparison preserves the actual source's when they troubled me wording.

relationship: Pleasing a neighbor: conduct and instruction
rationale: The psalm joins its neighbor and brother comparison with the statement that the speaker sought to please. Paul instructs each person to please a neighbor for that neighbor's good and edification; the connection concerns this stated conduct, without supplying a cause for the psalmist's mourning.

The enemies' gnashing teeth at the speaker has a narrative counterpart in Stephen's enraged hearers grinding their teeth at him. Both depict fierce hostility toward the person addressing or facing them.
Both pleas ask for rescue of the speaker's soul or only life and employ lions as an image of the threatening power. Psalm21 distributes the only-one and lion images across two adjacent units.
The promise to thank and praise the Lord in a great assembly corresponds to the promise to recount His name to brothers and sing hymns in the midst of the assembly.

Jesus applies the scriptural words about being hated without cause to His rejection. That same unprovoked hatred is named here; the comparison preserves John's fulfillment claim without asserting an exclusive source identification.

Peaceful speech conceals deceit in this verse. Psalm27 similarly describes people speaking peace to neighbors while harboring evils in their hearts, exposing the opposition between their words and purposes.

The enemies open their mouths and claim that their eyes have seen the desired disaster. Jerusalem's enemies likewise open their mouths, celebrate swallowing her, and say that they found and saw the awaited day.

The request that God awake and attend to the case corresponds to Psalm43's repeated call for the Lord to awake, arise and help an afflicted people. Both use awakening language within petitions for intervention.

Both speakers ask the Lord to judge their case according to righteousness. Here the appeal names God's righteousness; Psalm7 names the petitioner's righteousness and innocence, a significant difference in the stated ground.
The feared enemy boast, We have swallowed him, closely corresponds to the enemies' boast over Jerusalem, We have swallowed her. The object changes from an individual to the city.
The request that hostile boasters wear shame and humiliation closely matches the request that slanderers wear humiliation and wrap themselves in shame like a cloak.

Both lines invite a supportive group to rejoice and continually say that the Lord be magnified. Here they desire the servant's righteousness and peace; Psalm39 identifies seekers of God and lovers of His salvation.
Both speakers promise that their tongue will meditate on God's righteousness all day. Psalm70 adds the shame of enemies, while this verse pairs righteousness with continual praise.

The heading specifically calls David the Lord's servant. The Lord's message through Nathan addresses David as My servant, supplying the same named relationship without dating this psalm to that message.
Romans closes its scriptural indictment with no fear of God before their eyes, matching this description of the lawless person's lack of fear before his eyes.

The psalm identifies lawlessness and deceit in the wicked person's mouth. Romans' indictment similarly locates deceit in tongues and cursing and bitterness in the mouth, giving concrete forms of corrupt speech.
Both passages place the devising of evil upon beds. Micah expressly places the carrying out of the plans at daybreak.
Both lines pair God's mercy reaching heaven with His truth reaching the clouds, repeating the two attributes and their corresponding heights.

The Lord's saving humans and beasts corresponds to His question about sparing Nineveh with its many people and much livestock. Both expressly include animal life alongside human life in divine preservation.
Hope beneath God's wings is repeated in Psalm90, where divine overshadowing and protective truth accompany the assurance that the addressee will hope under His wings.

The abundance of God's house and torrent offered to drink have a related sanctuary image in Ezekiel: water flows from the house, grows into an uncrossable torrent, and gives life wherever it comes. The vision and praise poem retain different settings.

The psalm joins life originating with God and seeing by His light. John's prologue likewise joins life in the divine Word with light for humankind and identifies the true Light as illuminating every person.
The plea for mercy toward those knowing God and righteousness for the upright corresponds to Jeremiah's account of knowing the Lord who performs mercy, judgment and righteousness on earth.
The workers of lawlessness fall and cannot stand here. Proverbs contrasts the righteous person's repeated rising with the impious growing weak amid evils, distinguishing the outcomes of downfall.

Both instructions explicitly forbid envying people who do evil. Proverbs says not to rejoice over evildoers, while the psalm says not to be provoked to envy; the shared prohibition of envy is retained precisely.
The rapid passing of evildoers is compared to grass drying and plants falling. Isaiah uses withered grass and fallen flowers for all human flesh, contrasting this mortality with God's enduring word.
Trust and kindness accompany dwelling in a richly supplied land here. Deuteronomy similarly joins loving and obeying the Lord with life and blessing in the land being inherited.

The person delighting in the Lord receives the heart's requests; John describes confidence that God hears requests made according to His will. John's explicit qualification by God's will is preserved.
Revealing one's way to the Lord and hoping for His action corresponds to Psalm61's invitation to hope in God and pour out one's heart before Him as helper.

The promised emergence of righteousness like light and judgment like noon corresponds to Isaiah's righteousness going before the faithful and darkness becoming like noon after practical mercy toward the oppressed.
The prohibition of envy at a lawless person's prosperity addresses the very temptation Asaph confesses when he envied lawless people on seeing sinners' peace.
Abandoning anger and wrath so as not to act wickedly corresponds to James' instruction to be slow to anger because human anger does not accomplish God's righteousness.

Those waiting for the Lord inherit the land in contrast to evildoers' destruction. Isaiah similarly contrasts helpless objects carried away by wind with people holding fast to God acquiring land and inheriting His holy mountain.

The sinner disappears and his place cannot be found; Zophar likewise pictures the ungodly vanishing so completely that observers ask where he is and his place no longer perceives him. The comparison concerns that image within Zophar's speech.
Jesus' beatitude repeats the meek inheriting the earth, corresponding to the meek inheriting the land here. The psalm also adds their delight in abundant peace.
The sinner gnashing teeth at the righteous person is illustrated by Stephen's hearers angrily grinding their teeth at him before the assault narrated in Acts.
The Lord laughing at the plotting sinner corresponds to the One dwelling in heaven laughing at gathered hostile rulers. Both place God's derision over threatening human plans.
The sinners prepare weapons to slaughter the upright and needy. The gang's invitation in Proverbs likewise proposes bloodshed and the unjust destruction of a righteous person.

The enemy's sword is requested to enter his own heart. Proverbs similarly says that murderous lawless people store evils for themselves and take away their own life, reversing the intended benefit of their violence.

Both sayings prefer a small portion joined to a right relationship with God over great wealth without it. This psalm names righteousness versus sinners; Proverbs names fear of the Lord versus fearlessness.

Shattered sinners' arms are contrasted with sustained righteous people. Psalm74 likewise contrasts broken sinners' horns with raised righteous horns, using a different bodily image for opposed outcomes of strength.
The Lord knowing the ways of the blameless closely corresponds to His knowing the way of the righteous in Psalm1, where the opposing ungodly way perishes.

The enduring inheritance of the blameless has a counterpart in Peter's imperishable, unfading inheritance kept in heaven for people guarded by God's power. The earthly land context of the psalm and Peter's heavenly location remain distinct.
The promise that the righteous will be filled during famine is illustrated by the Lord sustaining Elijah, the widow and her children through flour and oil that do not run out before the rains.
The Lord's enemies vanish like smoke here; Psalm67 likewise requests that sinners vanish as smoke vanishes before God. Both apply the same disappearing-smoke image to hostile wickedness.

The psalm contrasts the sinner who fails to repay with the righteous person who has compassion and gives. Proverbs similarly contrasts the impious person's desires with the righteous person's unstinting mercy and compassion.

Both passages attach opposing outcomes to blessing and cursing another: inheritance versus destruction here, and God's blessing or curse toward those responding to Abram in Genesis. The psalm's pronoun him is not resolved into Abram's identity.
Both statements explicitly say that a person's steps are directed by the Lord. The psalm follows this with the Lord desiring his way; Proverbs follows it with a question about human understanding.
The righteous person can fall without being dashed down because the Lord supports him; Proverbs likewise says that the righteous can fall seven times and rise, distinguishing a fall from final ruin.

The speaker's observation concerns a righteous person not being abandoned and his offspring not seeking bread. Psalm111 similarly associates fear of the Lord with blessed offspring and a supplied household, expressing provision across generations.
The righteous person's continual mercy and lending correspond to Psalm111's kind person who has compassion and lends. Both join generosity of disposition with the concrete act of lending.
The command to turn aside from evil and do good appears in Peter's quoted instruction as well. This psalm continues with enduring dwelling, while Peter's sentence continues with seeking peace.
The Lord will not abandon His holy ones, while the lawless are driven out. Samuel similarly assures Israel that the Lord will not reject His people and then warns them against continuing in evil.
Both passages explicitly join righteous people, inheritance of the land, and enduring possession: the righteous dwell there age upon age here, and Isaiah's people inherit it for ever.
The righteous mouth meditating on wisdom corresponds to the righteous mouth dripping wisdom in Proverbs. Both identify wisdom as the characteristic product of righteous speech.
God's law in the heart accompanies steps that do not stumble. Psalm118 likewise places God's sayings in the heart with the stated purpose of avoiding sin, linking inward retention to conduct.

The sinner watches the righteous to kill him. Wisdom develops the same hostile plan: opponents lie in wait for the righteous, resent his different life, and resolve to condemn him to a shameful death.

The Lord will not abandon the righteous into the sinner's hands when judgment comes. Paul recounts being deserted at his defense while the Lord stood beside him, and looks toward final rescue into the heavenly kingdom.

Waiting for the Lord and keeping His way lead to inheritance of the land here. Isaiah likewise promises land and God's holy mountain to those holding fast to Him while exposing the helplessness of rival refuges.

The ungodly person's apparent greatness is likened to Lebanon's cedars. Ezekiel depicts Assyria as a tall Lebanese cypress before its destruction: different tree names, but the common image of imposing power destined to fall.
The speaker can no longer find the ungodly person's place. Zophar's image likewise describes the wicked as an unfindable dream whose former place no longer perceives him.
The instruction to guard innocence and look upon uprightness accompanies a remnant for the peaceful person. Proverbs similarly promises that good, innocent and upright people will remain in the land.
The destruction of the lawless and ungodly remnants corresponds to Proverbs' statement that ungodly ways perish from the land and the lawless are driven out of it.
The Lord is the righteous person's defender in a time of affliction here; Psalm9 calls Him the needy person's refuge and helper at fitting times in distress.
The Lord rescues and saves because they hoped in Him. Psalm90 voices the same causal assurance from God: because the person hoped in Him, He will rescue and shelter him.

The title explicitly associates this psalm with remembrance concerning the Sabbath. Psalm91's heading likewise identifies a psalm-song for the Sabbath day, preserving a particular worship designation rather than only shared authorship.
The entire petition against rebuke in fury and discipline in anger repeats the wording of Psalm6:2, including the two parallel divine actions and emotional terms.

The Lord's arrows lodged in the speaker correspond to Job's description of the Lord's arrows in his body. Both portray suffering through arrows from God; their surrounding accounts of personal culpability differ.
The speaker connects bodily and bone distress with sin and God's anger. Psalm 31 likewise places aging bones and God's heavy hand before an explicit confession of sin and forgiveness.

Lawless deeds rise above the speaker's head here. Ezra's confession similarly says the community's lawless deeds have multiplied above their heads and their offenses grown to heaven, using height to express overwhelming guilt.

The bruises that stink and rot because of folly correspond to Isaiah's wounded, bruised and inflamed portrayal of a sinful nation without dressings. The comparison concerns bodily imagery in confessions or accusations of wrongdoing.
Both speakers describe walking downcast while suffering. Here the speaker is bent down in misery; Psalm41 asks why he walks downcast under an enemy's oppression.

The declaration that there is no healing in the speaker's flesh repeats the same phrase from verse 4. The earlier line names God's anger and sins; this line adds loins filled with mockings, preserving the source's unusual wording within the repeated bodily lament.
The deeply humbled speaker roars from the groaning of his heart. Psalm6 similarly describes weariness through groaning, extending the lament into nights of tears upon the bed.

The speaker's desires and groaning are fully before God. Romans likewise connects groanings beyond words with the One searching hearts; there the Spirit is explicitly the intercessor helping human weakness.
Loss of strength and the eyes' light corresponds to Psalm12's plea for God to give light to the eyes lest the speaker sleep into death. One laments the loss, and the other asks its reversal.

The psalm places friends and neighbors opposite the sufferer and those nearest him far away. Job likewise describes withdrawn brothers, merciless friends and neighbors treating him as a foreigner; their precise behaviors differ.

The close acquaintances standing far away have a narrative counterpart in Jesus' acquaintances and the women watching from a distance. Luke describes these people remaining as witnesses to the suffering scene.

Those seeking the speaker's life use violence and meditate on deceptions. Mark likewise describes leaders seeking a way to seize Jesus by deceit and kill Him, a specific narrative parallel for the combination of deception and lethal intent.
The sufferer becomes like one unable to speak who does not open his mouth. Isaiah's afflicted servant is likewise described twice as not opening his mouth, with the silence of a lamb before shearers.

The speaker depicts his silence amid persecution by comparison with a person unable to speak. Matthew describes Jesus giving no answer to the accusations of the chief priests and elders, despite Pilate's question about their testimony.
The speaker has no rebukes in his mouth despite hostility. Peter describes Christ not returning reviling or threats when abused and suffering, while entrusting His cause to the just Judge.
Both passages connect the speaker's being shaken with enemies exulting over him and seek to prevent that outcome. Psalm12 supplies the corresponding boast that the enemy has prevailed.
The announcement of lawlessness corresponds to Psalm31's explicit confession of lawlessness to the Lord without concealing sin. Psalm31 also records the resulting forgiveness.
The enemies who unjustly hate the speaker multiply and grow stronger here. Psalm68 likewise describes numerous causeless haters and unjustly pursuing enemies becoming strong.

The complaint of evil repaid for good corresponds to Proverbs' warning that evils will remain in the house of one who repays evil instead of good. The psalm also supplies its own slander and rejected-corpse imagery.
The appeal for the Lord of salvation to attend to the speaker's aid corresponds to Psalm69's adjoining request for the Lord to save and for God to attend to his help.
Both headings combine the for-the-end designation, the name Jeduthun, and David's song or psalm. The shared named recipient makes the title comparison more specific than Davidic authorship alone.
The speaker places a guard on his mouth to avoid sinning with his tongue. Psalm140 explicitly asks the Lord to set a guard for the mouth and a restraining door around the lips.

Silence is followed by renewed pain here; Psalm31 similarly associates keeping silent with bones growing old amid continual crying. The local contexts differ: restraint before the sinner here and confession of sin in Psalm31.

The speaker's heart grew hot, and a fire will be kindled in his meditation, as the psalm moves from silence to speech. Jeremiah says he will no longer name the Lord or speak in His name, but describes a burning fire in his bones that he cannot bear.

The prayer asks God to reveal life's limit and number of days. Job states that a person's months are numbered with God and a divinely set time cannot be exceeded, supplying the same combination of counting and a boundary.
The speaker's short days and human vanity correspond to Psalm143's human being likened to futility and days passing like a shadow. Both use a brief span and insubstantial imagery for human life.

The person gathers treasure without knowing for whom he gathers it. Jesus' rich fool stores goods for years but is told his life is demanded that very night, facing God's question about whose the prepared possessions will be.
The confession that the speaker's existence comes from God corresponds to Paul's proclamation that God gives everyone life and breath and that in Him people live, move and exist.

The personal plea for rescue from all lawless deeds corresponds to the promise that the Lord will redeem Israel from all its lawless deeds. The scope changes from the individual to Israel while retaining comprehensive release from wrongdoing.
Becoming mute and not opening the mouth repeats the comparison with a person unable to speak who does not open his mouth. This verse explicitly attributes the restraint to God as maker.
The plea to remove scourges and the wasting force of God's hand corresponds to Job's request that God keep His hand away and not overwhelm him with terror.

The Lord's rebukes and discipline for lawlessness correspond to the instruction about receiving the Lord's discipline and correction. Proverbs explicitly supplies a loving father-and-son framework, while the psalm stresses human frailty.
Both prayers call the worshippers sojourners or resident strangers before God like all their fathers. Chronicles also compares earthly days to a shadow, matching this psalm's context of brief life.
Both speakers ask for a little relief before an irreversible departure from mortal life. The psalm says before I depart and no longer exist; Job speaks of going without return to a dark land.

Being lifted from muddy slime and set on a rock reverses the situation in Psalm68, where the sufferer is stuck in deep mud without firm ground. The shared image joins mire with the presence or absence of stable footing.
God gives a new song after rescue here; Psalm97 calls for a new song because the Lord has done wonders and won salvation. Both connect new praise with saving action.
Both pronounce blessed the person whose hope or trust is in the Lord. The psalm additionally rejects vanities and false frenzies, while Jeremiah's context contrasts dependence on human power.
The speaker cannot number God's many wonders and purposes. Eliphaz likewise describes the Lord's great, extraordinary works as beyond numbering; the connection is to this statement within his speech.

Hebrews quotes the rejection of sacrifice, offering, burnt offerings and sin offerings. This Psalms text says ears were prepared, while Hebrews says a body was prepared; both exact wordings are preserved without harmonizing them.
Hebrews repeats the declaration of coming and the scroll of the book written concerning the speaker. Those are the distinctive clauses of this psalm unit before the following statement of God's will.

Hebrews quotes coming to do God's will and interprets that will through Jesus Christ's once-for-all bodily offering. The psalm's additional law within my belly wording remains specific to this source.

The testimony of proclaiming righteousness in a great assembly corresponds to the pledge to declare God's name among brothers and sing hymns within the assembly. Both locate proclamation in a gathered community, with different past and future wording.

The speaker has not hidden divine righteousness, truth and salvation from the congregation. Paul likewise says he held back nothing beneficial and taught publicly, bearing witness to repentance toward God and faith in Jesus.

The plea names God's compassions, mercy and truth as sustaining the speaker. The Lord's self-proclamation to Moses names Him compassionate, merciful, abundant in mercy and true, supplying the same cluster of attributes.

Lawless deeds overtake and overwhelm the speaker here. Psalm37 similarly describes them rising above his head and weighing like a heavy load, expressing transgression as a burden exceeding his strength.
The plea for the Lord to rescue and attend to helping the speaker closely corresponds to Psalm69's request for the Lord to save and for God to attend to his help.
Both prayers ask that seekers of the speaker's life be ashamed and that those wishing him evil turn backward in disgrace, retaining the same paired enemy groups and reversals.
The enemies' Well done taunt and requested immediate shame correspond to Psalm69's Well, Well taunt and requested turning back immediately in shame.
Both verses invite all who seek God to rejoice and all who love His salvation to continually declare that God or the Lord be magnified.
Both speakers identify themselves as poor and needy, call God helper and rescuer or defender, and end with the request not to delay.

relationship: care for the poor and divine repayment
rationale: The blessing and promised rescue for someone attentive to the poor correspond to Proverbs' assurance that God repays the person showing mercy to the poor.
The request that the Lord not hand the person into enemy hands corresponds to the assurance that the Lord will not abandon the righteous into the sinner's hands when he faces judgment.
The request for God's help on a bed of pain corresponds to James' instruction to pray over a sick person and his assurance that the Lord will raise that person up.
The petition joins mercy and healing of the soul with confession of sin. Psalm102 likewise places God's gracious treatment of lawless deeds beside His healing of diseases.

The enemies here wish the sufferer's death and the loss of his name. Psalm 108 likewise voices a wish for a person's name and memorial to be erased. The comparison concerns this imprecatory wording without equating the persons or settling the speaking roles of every imprecation.

The visitor speaks vainly while gathering lawlessness in his heart, then goes outside and speaks. Proverbs exposes an enemy's agreeable lips concealing deceitful purposes in his heart and hidden enmity.
The enemies whisper together and devise evils against the speaker. Matthew gives a concrete parallel of leaders gathering together and taking counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill Him.

Jesus quotes Scripture about the person eating His bread lifting a heel against Him. This psalm describes a trusted companion eating the speaker's loaves and magnifying treachery; John applies the meal-and-betrayal pattern to Jesus' impending betrayal.

The prayer for mercy and being raised up corresponds to Psalm 29's testimony of crying to the Lord, being healed and having the soul brought up from Hades. The shared restoration theme does not identify the two experiences as one event.
The speaker recognizes divine favor because his enemy will not rejoice over him. Psalm29 likewise praises God for taking the speaker up without gladdening his enemies over him.

Being sustained in innocence and established before God corresponds to Psalm16's expectation of appearing before God's face in righteousness. Both join right standing with access to the divine presence.
Both doxologies bless the Lord as Israel's God, extend the blessing across the ages, and conclude with the doubled May it be response.
Chronicles repeats the blessing of the Lord, Israel's God, from age to age, followed by the people's Amen. It provides a communal worship counterpart to this psalm's closing doxology.
